title: REGEX Functions
goal: Test, extract and replace text with REGEXTEST, REGEXEXTRACT and REGEXREPLACE using beginner patterns, and know how the old LEFT/MID/FIND way compares.

steps.text:
These notes mix words and numbers. The invoice number sits in a different place each time, and it's a different length: 4821, 17, 5017…

The old way needs `FIND`, `MID` and a guess about lengths. Microsoft 365 has **regular expressions** (“regex”): a tiny code that describes a pattern. Three functions use it:

• `REGEXTEST(text, pattern)`: is the pattern in the text? TRUE or FALSE
• `REGEXEXTRACT(text, pattern)`: pull out the first match
• `REGEXREPLACE(text, pattern, replacement)`: swap every match

In ==B2== you'd type `=REGEXEXTRACT(A2, "\d+")` and fill down. The text goes first, the pattern second, in quotes.

Honest note: this practice sheet can't run regex, so you'll do the same jobs the old way and predict what the regex gives.

Six pieces are enough to start:

• `\d`: one digit, 0 to 9
• `[0-9]`: the same thing, written as a range
• `+`: “one or more” of the piece before it, so `\d+` is a whole number
• `[A-Z]`: one capital letter
• `.`: any one character
• `^` and `$`: the start and the end of the text

The table shows what `REGEXEXTRACT` would return. Regex is **case-sensitive** by default, so `[A-Z]` ignores lowercase. If nothing matches, REGEXEXTRACT gives #N/A.

steps.prompt: Which pattern pulls just the digits out of **Invoice 4821 paid**?
steps.explain: `\d+` finds a run of digits wherever it sits, here 4821. Only the pattern changes; the formula shape stays the same.
wrongFeedback: `[A-Z]+` looks for capital letters. In this note it would only find the “I” of Invoice.
`^` means “at the very start”. The digits are in the middle, so there's no match and you'd get #N/A.

steps.prompt:
First the **old way**, to see why regex is a relief. The number starts right after the first space and is 4 digits long.

In ==B2==, use `FIND` to locate the space, `MID` to take 4 characters after it, and wrap everything in `VALUE` to turn it into a number.
steps.explain: 4821. It works, but only because every number here has exactly 4 digits. That is a guess baked into the formula.

wrongFeedback.parseError: Check the brackets and commas: `MID(text, start, length)`.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Use MID (and FIND) to cut the number out.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: FIND gives the position of the space; add 1 to start at the first digit, then take 4 characters.

clues: MID(A2, position of first digit, 4). The first digit is FIND(" ",A2)+1.

steps.prompt: You fill that formula down to row 3, **Invoice 17 paid**. MID still takes exactly 4 characters. What does `B3` show?
steps.explain: MID grabs “17 p” and VALUE can't turn that into a number. The regex `\d+` doesn't count characters; it takes however many digits are there and returns 17.
wrongFeedback: The formula doesn't know where the number ends: it takes exactly 4 characters, “17 p”.
“17 p” is what MID alone returns. But VALUE wraps it, and it can't read letters, so you get #VALUE!.
clues: How many characters does MID take, and how many does “17” have?

steps.prompt:
A rule checks each product code with `=REGEXTEST(A2, "^[A-Z]")`: TRUE if the code **starts with a capital letter**.

Click the **one code** that would get FALSE, then press [[Enter]].
steps.wrongFeedback: Look for the code whose first letter is **lowercase**: `[A-Z]` only accepts capitals.
clues: Four codes start with a letter; one of them isn't a capital.

steps.prompt:
`=REGEXTEST(A2, "^Paid")` is TRUE only when the note **starts** with Paid. Do the old way in ==B2==: compare the first 4 characters of the note with Paid.

Watch the note: it says **Unpaid**.
steps.explain: FALSE: “Unpa” isn't “Paid”. A search for “paid” anywhere would say TRUE, but the `^` in the pattern means start only, and `LEFT` checks the start too.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Use LEFT to take the first 4 characters.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: “Unpaid” contains “paid” in the middle, but it doesn't start with it. Check only the first 4 characters.

clues: LEFT(A2,4) gives the first four characters. Compare that to "Paid".

steps.explain: `^C` starts with C, `.` is exactly **one** any-character, `T$` ends with T. COT fits; CT has no middle character; COAT has two.
wrongFeedback: `.` stands for exactly one character, and CT has none between C and T.
COAT has two characters between C and T, but `.` allows just one.
clues: Count the characters: C, one of anything, T.

steps.prompt:
`=REGEXEXTRACT(A3, "[A-Z]+")` returns the capital letters at the start of a code. Do it the old way in ==B3==: take everything **before the dash**.

The airline code has a different length from the city code above it.
steps.explain: GO. `LEFT(A3,3)` would wrongly give “GO-”. Cutting at the dash works for any length, just like `[A-Z]+` does.

wrongFeedback.parseError: Check the quotes around the dash.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: You want only the letters before the dash. Taking a fixed 3 characters includes the dash.

clues: TEXTBEFORE(A3,"-") returns what comes before the dash.

steps.explain: `\d+` treats 12 and 345 each as one whole number, and REGEXREPLACE replaces **every** match by default. So each number becomes a single #.
wrongFeedback: REGEXREPLACE replaces every match unless you ask for just one, so 345 changes too.
`\d` (without +) would give that, one # per digit. With `+`, each whole number becomes a single #.
clues: How many separate runs of digits are in the text?

steps.prompt:
`=REGEXREPLACE(A2, "-", "")` swaps the dash for nothing. The classic old way is `SUBSTITUTE`.

In ==B2==, clean this phone number so it has no dash.
steps.explain: 9876543210. For one fixed character, SUBSTITUTE is enough. Regex earns its keep when the thing to replace is a pattern, like “any run of digits”.

wrongFeedback.parseError: Check the quotes: `SUBSTITUTE(text, old, new)`, and the new text is empty quotes.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Use SUBSTITUTE to swap the dash for nothing.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: The result should be the ten digits with no dash.

clues: SUBSTITUTE(A2, "-", "") replaces the dash with empty text.

steps.prompt: The note in ==A2== hides an invoice number. Put just the invoice number, as a **number** you could add up, in ==B2==.
steps.explain: 7305. You cut after “invoice ”, then before the next space, then turned the text into a number. In a regex-enabled Excel it's `=VALUE(REGEXEXTRACT(A2,"\d+"))`; REGEXEXTRACT always returns text, so VALUE matters for maths.

wrongFeedback.wrongValue: You need only the digits 7305, and as a real number (right-aligned), not the whole note and not text.

clues: Cut the text after “invoice ”, then before the next space, then turn it into a number.
